newsitem.title: USA: O.J. Simpson to take witness stand for first time.
newsitem.headline: O.J. Simpson to take witness stand for first time.

text.p: O.J. Simpson was due to take the witness stand for the first time on Friday, nearly 2-1/2 years after his ex-wife and her friend were murdered, to tell a civil court jury what he was doing on the night of the killings.

The former football hero's testimony was seen as pivotal in a case where the families of the victims -- defying a criminal court jury's verdict that he was not guilty of the June 12, 1994, murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman -- are suing him for wrongful death and seeking substantial financial damages.
According to legal experts, Simpson's demeanor on the witness stand could either condemn or exonerate him in the eyes of the jury.
"This will be the defining moment of the trial," said Peter Arenella, a law professor at the University of California at Los Angeles.

Arenella said the predominantly white jury, chosen from Los Angeles' affluent west side area, would probably disregard the scientific DNA evidence linking Simpson's blood and those of the victims to blood at the crime scene outside Nicole Brown Simpson's Brentwood condominium, where the murders took place.
Blood from the victims was also found mingled with Simpson's blood inside his white Ford Bronco, according to police evidence, as well as in socks found in his mansion.
"The jury will probably view the evidence through the prism of Simpson's credibility," Arenella said.
Simpson did not testify at his criminal trial but under California law he can be called by either side at the civil trial.

Arenella said that in calling Simpson, the attorneys for the plaintiffs were taking a calculated risk. "If Mr. Simpson handles the domestic violence evidence more forthrightly than he has in the past, Simpson will score points and the jury will gain a positive image of Simpson."
Attorneys for the plaintiffs have brought up several instances in which police were called by Nicole Brown Simpson complaining she was either being threatened or beaten by Simpson.

The mostly black jury in Simpson's criminal case said that in rendering their not-guilty verdict they had all but disregarded the DNA evidence as being too complicated and mind-boggling, with experts putting the odds at billions to one the blood was anyone's but Simpson's and the victims'.
At issue is where Simpson was at the time of the murders, put by lawyers for the plaintiffs at around 10:40 p.m. on the night of June 12, 1994.

In sworn depositions given earlier this year to lawyers for both sides in the case, Simpson said he was variously chipping golf balls out of a sand trap in the grounds of his mansion, taking a dog for a walk, reading, sleeping and taking a shower.

Previous testimony has shown that no one saw Simpson between shortly after 9:00 p.m., when he and his house guest, Brian "Kato" Kaelin, returned from getting a hamburger, and about 10:55 p.m. when he was seen by limousine driver Allan Park, who arrived to take him to the airport for an overnight trip to Chicago.

Lawyers for the plaintiffs have attempted to establish that Nicole Brown Simpson and Goldman were stabbed to death in a matter of seconds at around 10:40 p.m., giving Simpson time to commit the murders outside his ex-wife's condominium and still return to his mansion two miles (three km) away in time to take the limousine.
Simpson's lawyers have argued the murders took about 15 minutes to commit, thereby eliminating the former athlete as the killer.
